about: Engineering Drawing is the Lent Term, manual-drawing half of the Part IA Drawing course in Cambridge's Engineering Tripos (Computer-aided Design is the Michaelmas half). The 2026-27 Part IA guide says it covers how 3D objects are represented on 2D surfaces, with each drawing session opening with a lecture and work handed in at the end of the session. The most recent syllabus page that could be read (2024-25) lists five areas in order, each with its own workbook: orthographic projection, isometric drawing, auxiliary views, sectioning and dimensioning. It is coursework, not part of a written paper: the 2026-27 credit notice gives 3 marks for satisfactory effort on each of five workbooks (15 marks, qualifying 15, standard credit).

notes.body:
Orthographic projection is the backbone of the Lent drawing course. It represents a 3D object with several 2D views, each made by projecting the object onto a plane with parallel projectors that are perpendicular to that plane. Because there is no perspective, distances parallel to the plane of a view are shown at true length.

Kinds of drawing
- Pictorial drawings (for example isometric) show the object in one view and are easy to read, but most dimensions are distorted.
- Multi-view orthographic drawings are harder to read at first, but every feature can be shown at true size and dimensioned without ambiguity. Formal engineering drawings are almost always orthographic.

Line types (BS 8888, which uses the ISO 128 line conventions)
- Continuous thick: visible edges and outlines.
- Continuous thin: dimension lines, projection lines, leader lines and hatching.
- Dashed thin: hidden edges.
- Chain thin (long dash, short dash): centre lines and lines of symmetry.
- Chain thin, thick at the ends and at changes of direction: the trace of a cutting plane.

How the views relate
- The front view (front elevation) shows width and height; the plan (view from above) shows width and depth; an end view shows depth and height.
- Views share dimensions, so they must line up: front view and plan are aligned vertically (same width), front view and end view are aligned horizontally (same height). Depth is carried between plan and end view, for example with a 45° mitre line or by measuring.

The two layout conventions
- First angle: imagine the object between you and the projection plane. Each view is placed on the opposite side of the front view from the side it was viewed from. The plan goes below the front view; the view from the left goes to the right of the front view.
- Third angle: imagine the projection plane between you and the object. Each view is placed on the same side as it was viewed from. The plan goes above the front view; the view from the left goes on the left.
- First angle has traditionally been used in the UK and Europe and third angle in North America. BS 8888 allows either, but the drawing must show the standard projection symbol (a truncated cone drawn in two views) so the reader knows which was used.

Principal views
- There are six principal views (front, rear, top, bottom, left, right), but you draw only as many as are needed to define the part, usually two or three.
- Choose as the front view the one that shows the most characteristic shape with the fewest hidden lines, and orient the part in its natural or functional position.

Why second and fourth angle are not used
- If you place the object in the second or fourth quadrant and unfold the planes, the plan and the front view land on the same side of the reference line and overlap, so the drawing becomes unreadable.

Exam tips: before drawing, decide the projection convention and check every pair of views shares the right dimension. When reading a drawing, find the projection symbol first; mixing up first and third angle turns left into right and top into bottom.

Isometric views are pictorial: they show three faces of an object at once, which makes them good for sketching ideas and for communicating shape quickly. They are also a test of spatial reasoning, because you often have to convert between an isometric view and orthographic views.

What an isometric view is
- It is an orthographic projection taken looking along a body diagonal of a cube, so the three principal axes are equally inclined to the viewing direction.
- On the page the three axes appear 120° apart. With the vertical axis drawn vertical, the other two run at 30° to the horizontal.
- In a true isometric projection every length along an axis is foreshortened by the same factor, √(2/3) ≈ 0.816.
- In an isometric drawing (what you normally sketch) you ignore the foreshortening and measure true lengths along the axes. The result has exactly the same shape but is about 1.22 times (1/0.816) larger than the true projection.

Isometric and non-isometric lines
- Lines parallel to the axes are isometric lines and can be measured directly.
- Sloping edges are not drawn to scale. Locate their end points by measuring along the axes, then join them.
- A reliable sketching method is to draw the enclosing box first, then cut away material and add features.

Circles, cylinders and spheres
- A circle on any face appears as an ellipse. The ratio of minor to major axis is 1/√3 ≈ 0.58 on every face.
- The major axis is perpendicular to the axis of the hole or cylinder. For a circle on the top face, the major axis is horizontal.
- The ellipse touches the midpoints of the sides of the rhombus (the isometric square) that encloses the circle. This gives a quick way to sketch it.
- In an isometric drawing at full axis scale, a circle of diameter D appears with a major axis of about 1.22D and a minor axis of about 0.71D. For D = 50 mm that is about 61.2 mm by 35.4 mm.
- A cylinder is drawn as two ellipses joined by tangent lines parallel to its axis.
- A sphere's outline is a circle. In a true isometric projection its diameter equals the sphere's diameter; in an isometric drawing it is scaled up by the same 1.22 factor as everything else.

Locations, movements and forces
- Positions can be described by distances along the three axes from a reference corner.
- Linear movements and forces are shown by arrows parallel to the relevant axis. Rotations are shown by arrows following an elliptical arc in the plane of rotation.

Dimetric and trimetric views
- In a dimetric view two axes share the same scale and the third is different. In a trimetric view all three scales differ.
- These views can look more natural or emphasise a particular face, at the cost of more awkward measurement.

Exam tips: get the ellipse orientation right by asking which axis the hole runs along; the major axis is always perpendicular to it. When converting orthographic to isometric, build the enclosing box first and transfer every point by measuring along axes.

Principal views show a surface at true shape only if the surface is parallel to one of the principal planes. Auxiliary views solve the problem of inclined and oblique surfaces by projecting onto an extra plane chosen to suit the feature.

Inclined and oblique surfaces
- An inclined surface is perpendicular to one principal plane but tilted to the other two. In one principal view it appears as an edge (a line); in the other two it is foreshortened.
- An oblique surface is tilted to all three principal planes, so it is foreshortened in every principal view.

Primary auxiliary views
- Start from the view in which the inclined surface appears as an edge.
- Draw a reference (fold) line parallel to that edge. Project lines from each corner perpendicular to the edge view.
- Measure the distance of each point from the reference line in a related view (one adjacent to the view you are projecting from) and transfer those distances along the projectors.
- The result shows the inclined surface at true shape.

Four core rules (descriptive geometry)
- True length: a line appears at true length in a view whose plane is parallel to it. You can tell, because in an adjacent view the line runs parallel to the reference line.
- Point view: looking along a true-length line (projecting parallel to it) makes the line appear as a point.
- Edge view: a plane appears as an edge in any view where a line lying in it appears as a point.
- True shape: a plane appears at true shape in a view projected perpendicular to its edge view.

Oblique surfaces need two steps
- First auxiliary view: choose a line in the plane that is true length in an existing view (for example a horizontal line, which is true length in plan). View along it to get an edge view of the plane.
- Secondary auxiliary view: project perpendicular to that edge view to get the true shape.

Partial auxiliary views
- An auxiliary view shows other features foreshortened, which adds clutter. It is normal to draw only the inclined feature in the auxiliary view and leave the rest out.

Forces and moments
- A force drawn in space appears at true length (its true magnitude to scale) only in a view parallel to it.
- Looking along the axis of a moment makes the axis a point, and the rotation then appears in its true plane.

Worked example
- A line AB has components Δx = 30 mm, Δy = 40 mm and Δz = 120 mm (z vertical).
- Its plan length is √(30² + 40²) = 50 mm and its true length is √(30² + 40² + 120²) = √16900 = 130 mm.
- Its angle to the horizontal plane is tan⁻¹(120/50) ≈ 67.4°. An auxiliary view projected from the plan, with the reference line parallel to the plan of AB, shows AB at 130 mm and this angle directly.

Isometric as an auxiliary view
- An isometric projection is simply a secondary auxiliary view of a cube taken looking along a body diagonal, so that the diagonal appears as a point.

Exam tips: always label the reference lines and points consistently (for example a, a′, a1) and measure transferred distances from the correct reference line; most errors come from using the wrong related view.

Complicated internal detail drawn with hidden lines quickly becomes unreadable. Sectioning shows the inside of a part by imagining it cut by a plane and removing the material between the viewer and that plane.

Hidden detail
- Hidden edges are shown with thin dashed lines.
- Use them only where they help. Leave them out when they add confusion or when another view or a section shows the feature clearly.
- In a section view, hidden detail behind the cutting plane is normally omitted.

Presenting a section view
- The cutting plane is shown in an adjacent view by a thin chain line made thick at its ends and at any change of direction.
- Arrows at each end show the direction of viewing, and letters label the section (for example A–A). The section view carries the same label.
- Cut solid material is hatched with thin, evenly spaced lines, usually at 45°. Surfaces that are behind the cutting plane but not cut are drawn as visible outlines, not hatched.
- One part keeps the same hatching in every section. Adjacent parts in an assembly are hatched in different directions or with different spacing.

What is not hatched
- When a cutting plane passes along their length, conventionally items such as shafts, bolts, nuts, pins, keys, rivets, balls and rollers, and also ribs, webs and spokes, are shown unsectioned. Hatching them would add nothing and could suggest a solid region where there is none.

Special sections
- Full section: the plane cuts right through the part.
- Half section: for symmetrical parts, one half is drawn in section and the other as an outside view, divided by the centre line.
- Offset section: the cutting plane is stepped to pass through features that are not in line. The steps are not shown in the section view itself.
- Partial (local or broken-out) section: only a small region is sectioned, bounded by a thin freehand or zigzag break line.
- Revolved section: the cross-section of an arm or rib is rotated 90° and drawn in place on the view, in thin outline.
- Removed section: the cross-section is drawn away from the view and labelled, so it does not clutter the view.
- Successive sections: a series of removed sections along a member whose shape changes, such as a tapered arm or a hook.

Auxiliary sections
- If the cutting plane is inclined, project the section as an auxiliary view perpendicular to the cutting plane. That shows the cut face at true shape.

Sectioning in isometric
- A pictorial section usually removes a quarter or a half of the part. Cut faces are hatched, with the hatching on each cut face drawn in a clearly different direction.

Thin material
- Material too thin to hatch, such as sheet metal, gaskets or thin plates, is shown filled in solid. Leave a small white gap between adjacent thin parts so they can be told apart.

Exam tips: check that every cut surface in your section is hatched and that nothing behind the plane is hatched. A missing arrow or label on the cutting plane is a common, easily avoided loss of marks.

A drawing is only useful for manufacture if it defines size completely and unambiguously. Dimensioning is about giving exactly the information needed, in a form that reflects how the part works and how it will be made and inspected.

Elements of a dimension
- Projection (extension) lines: thin lines extended from the feature, with a small gap from the outline and running a little beyond the dimension line.
- Dimension line: a thin line with arrowheads that touch the projection lines.
- Value: in millimetres unless the drawing states otherwise.
- Leader line: a thin line pointing to a feature, used for notes and for diameters or radii.

Principles of dimensioning
- Dimension each feature once only, and give only the dimensions needed to define the part fully.
- Put each dimension on the view that shows that feature's shape most clearly.
- Avoid dimensioning to hidden lines. Keep dimensions outside the outline where possible.
- Do not use an outline or centre line as a dimension line.
- Dimension functionally important sizes directly, measured from a datum that matters to how the part fits and works.

Under- and over-dimensioning
- Under-dimensioned: some size or position is missing, so the part cannot be made uniquely.
- Over-dimensioned: a size is given twice, for example three step lengths of 20, 30 and 15 mm and also the overall length of 65 mm. Once each size has a tolerance, the closed chain can contradict itself, and it is unclear which size governs.
- Leave one dimension in the chain out. If a redundant size is useful for information, it can be shown as an auxiliary dimension in brackets, which is not toleranced.

Accounting for dimensional variation
- No part is made to an exact size. A tolerance states how much a dimension may vary, for example 20 ± 0.1 mm, meaning any size from 19.9 to 20.1 mm is acceptable. These extremes are the limits of size.
- Chain dimensioning (each feature from the previous one) lets tolerances accumulate. With 20 ± 0.1, 30 ± 0.1 and 15 ± 0.1 in a chain, the overall length can be anywhere from 64.7 to 65.3 mm in the worst case, that is ± 0.3 mm.
- Parallel (datum or baseline) dimensioning measures every feature from one datum. Each feature's position then varies by only its own tolerance, but the distance between two features can vary by the sum of both, ± 0.2 mm here.
- So choose the dimensioning scheme according to which sizes matter: dimension the critical size directly so it receives the tolerance, and let a non-critical size absorb the accumulated variation.

Fits
- Where parts mate, the limits of a hole and a shaft set the fit. For a hole of 20.00 to 20.05 mm and a shaft of 19.95 to 19.98 mm, the clearance ranges from 20.00 − 19.98 = 0.02 mm (tightest) to 20.05 − 19.95 = 0.10 mm (loosest). That is a clearance fit.

Exam tips: for any tolerance question, write down both limits of every size and work out the worst cases explicitly (largest minus smallest and smallest minus largest). Then check that each feature is dimensioned exactly once.

cards.b: Representing a 3D object by several 2D views, each made with parallel projectors perpendicular to the projection plane, so lengths parallel to that plane appear at true size.

cards.f: First-angle projection: where does the plan go?
cards.b: Below the front view. In first angle each view is placed on the opposite side of the front view from where it was seen; the view from the left goes on the right.

cards.f: Third-angle projection: where does the plan go?
cards.b: Above the front view. In third angle each view is placed on the side it was seen from; the view from the left goes on the left.
A thin dashed line.
A thin chain line (long dash, short dash).

cards.f: Line type for a cutting plane
cards.b: A thin chain line made thick at its ends and at changes of direction, with arrows showing the viewing direction.

cards.f: Which dimension do the front view and plan share?
cards.b: Width. They are aligned vertically; front view and end view share height (aligned horizontally); plan and end view share depth.

cards.f: Why are second- and fourth-angle projections not used?
cards.b: When the planes are unfolded, the plan and front view fall on the same side of the reference line and overlap, making the drawing unreadable.

cards.f: Angle between isometric axes on the page
cards.b: 120°. With the vertical axis vertical, the other two axes run at 30° to the horizontal.
√(2/3) ≈ 0.816 along each of the three axes.
An isometric drawing uses true lengths along the axes, so it is the same shape as the projection but about 1.22 times larger.
A line not parallel to any isometric axis. It is not at true length, so it is drawn by locating its end points along the axes and joining them.
Its major axis is perpendicular to the axis of the hole or cylinder; for a circle on the top face the major axis is horizontal.

cards.f: Minor-to-major axis ratio of an isometric ellipse
cards.b: 1/√3 ≈ 0.58, on every face.
Dimetric: two axes share a scale and the third differs. Trimetric: all three axes have different scales.
To show an inclined or oblique feature at true shape by projecting onto a plane parallel to it.
Inclined: perpendicular to one principal plane and tilted to the others (seen as an edge in one view). Oblique: tilted to all three principal planes.

cards.f: How do you know a line is true length in a view?
cards.b: In an adjacent view the line runs parallel to the reference (fold) line between the two views.

cards.f: How do you get an edge view of a plane?
cards.b: Find a view in which a line lying in the plane is a point, by looking along a true-length line in that plane.

cards.f: Why does an oblique surface need a secondary auxiliary view?
cards.b: No principal view shows it as an edge, so a first auxiliary view is needed to get the edge view, then a second, perpendicular to that edge, gives the true shape.
An auxiliary view showing only the inclined feature, leaving out the rest of the part, which would appear foreshortened and cluttered.

cards.f: Isometric projection as an auxiliary view
cards.b: It is a secondary auxiliary view of a cube taken along a body diagonal, so the diagonal appears as a point.

cards.f: Usual hatching for a cut surface
cards.b: Thin, evenly spaced lines, usually at 45°.

cards.f: Hatching adjacent parts in an assembly section
cards.b: Use a different direction or spacing for each adjacent part; keep the same hatching for one part in every section.

cards.f: Items conventionally not hatched when cut lengthwise
cards.b: Shafts, bolts, nuts, pins, keys, rivets, balls and rollers, plus ribs, webs and spokes.
For a symmetrical part: half is drawn in section and half as an outside view, separated by the centre line.
The cutting plane is stepped to pass through features not in line; the steps are not shown in the section view.
Revolved: cross-section rotated 90° and drawn in place on the view. Removed: cross-section drawn away from the view and labelled.
Fill it in solid rather than hatching, leaving a small gap between adjacent thin parts.
Giving a size more than once, e.g. every step length plus the overall length; with tolerances the closed chain can contradict itself.
Leaving out a size or position, so the part cannot be made uniquely from the drawing.
A redundant dimension given for information only, shown in brackets and not toleranced.
19.9 mm and 20.1 mm.
Tolerances accumulate: n chained sizes each ± t give a worst-case overall variation of ± nt.
All features dimensioned from one datum; each position varies only by its own tolerance, but the distance between two features can vary by the sum of both.
A fit where the smallest hole is larger than the largest shaft, so there is always clearance.

questions.q: A drawing shows the plan below the front view and the view from the left placed to the right of the front view. Which projection is it?
questions.why: In first angle each view goes on the opposite side from where it was seen: plan below, view from the left on the right. Third angle would put the plan above and the left view on the left. Isometric is a single pictorial view, and second angle is not used because the views overlap.

questions.q: Which pair of orthographic views must be aligned horizontally because they share the object's height?
questions.why: The front view and end view both show height, so they line up horizontally. Front view and plan share width (vertical alignment); plan and end view share depth, carried across with a mitre line; plan and underside both show width and depth, not height.

questions.q: Explain the difference between first-angle and third-angle orthographic projection, and state how a reader can tell which has been used on a drawing.
markScheme: First angle: object imagined between viewer and projection plane (1).
First angle layout: plan below front view, view from left placed to the right (1).
Third angle: projection plane imagined between viewer and object (1).
Third angle layout: plan above front view, view from left placed on the left (1).
The projection symbol (truncated cone in two views) on the drawing states the method (1).
questions.modelAnswer: In first-angle projection the object is imagined to sit between the observer and the projection plane, so each view is projected through the object onto the plane behind it. When the planes are unfolded, each view ends up on the opposite side of the front view from where it was seen: the plan sits below the front view and the view from the left sits on the right. In third-angle projection the projection plane is imagined between the observer and the object, so each view stays on the side it was seen from: the plan is above the front view and the view from the left is on the left. Both are allowed by BS 8888, so every drawing carries the standard projection symbol, a truncated cone drawn in two views, which tells the reader which convention applies.

questions.q: A 40 mm diameter hole is drilled vertically into the top face of a block. In an isometric drawing at full axis scale, which best describes the hole's outline?
options: An ellipse with a horizontal major axis of about 49 mm and minor axis of about 28 mm
An ellipse with a vertical major axis of about 49 mm and minor axis of about 28 mm
An ellipse with a horizontal major axis of 40 mm and minor axis of about 23 mm
questions.why: Circles on isometric faces appear as ellipses, so it is not a circle. The major axis is perpendicular to the hole's vertical axis, so it is horizontal, not vertical. In an isometric drawing at full axis scale everything is about 1.22 times the true isometric projection, so the major axis is about 1.22 × 40 ≈ 49 mm and the minor about 0.71 × 40 ≈ 28 mm (ratio 1/√3). The 40 mm by 23 mm ellipse has the right orientation and ratio but is the size in a true isometric projection, where the major axis equals the diameter; it forgets that the drawing measures full lengths along the axes and so is scaled up.

questions.q: In an isometric drawing, which lines can be measured directly at their true (drawing-scale) length?
options: Lines parallel to any of the three isometric axes
questions.why: Isometric lines, parallel to one of the three axes, are drawn to scale. Sloping (non-isometric) lines are distorted, so not all lines can be measured; vertical lines are only one of the three measurable directions; 45° is the angle of the receding axis in oblique (cavalier or cabinet) drawing, not an isometric axis, so 45° lines have no special status here.

questions.q: A cylinder of diameter 30 mm stands with its axis vertical. Describe how you would sketch it in an isometric drawing, giving the approximate sizes and orientation of the ellipses.
markScheme: Top and bottom circles drawn as ellipses (1).
Major axes horizontal, i.e. perpendicular to the vertical cylinder axis (1).
Major axis about 1.22 × 30 ≈ 36.7 mm; minor axis about 0.71 × 30 ≈ 21.2 mm (ratio 1/√3) (1).
Ellipses constructed in, and touching the midpoints of, an isometric square (rhombus) of side 30 mm (1).
Ellipses joined by two vertical tangent lines; hidden half of the bottom ellipse omitted or dashed (1).
questions.modelAnswer: Draw a vertical axis and, at the top and bottom, an isometric square (a rhombus) of side 30 mm with sides along the two 30° axes. Each circle becomes an ellipse inscribed in its rhombus, touching the midpoints of the four sides. Because the cylinder's axis is vertical, each ellipse's major axis is horizontal. At full axis scale the major axis is about 1.22 × 30 ≈ 36.7 mm and the minor axis about 0.71 × 30 ≈ 21.2 mm, a ratio of 1/√3. Finally join the two ellipses with vertical tangent lines at the ends of the major axes. Draw the rear half of the bottom ellipse dashed, or leave it out in a sketch.

questions.q: In a two-view drawing, line AB appears parallel to the reference line in the front view. What can you conclude?
options: AB is true length in the front view
AB is true length in the plan
AB appears as a point in the plan
AB is perpendicular to the horizontal plane
questions.why: If a line is parallel to the reference line in one view, it is parallel to the plane of the adjacent view, so AB is true length in the plan. Saying it is true length in the front view confuses the two views: that would need AB to appear parallel to the reference line in the plan. AB would appear as a point in the plan only if it were vertical, and being parallel to the reference line in the front view means it is horizontal, so it cannot be perpendicular to the horizontal plane.

questions.q: What is the minimum number of successive auxiliary views needed to show an oblique plane at true shape, starting from standard principal views?
questions.why: An oblique plane is not seen as an edge in any principal view. A first auxiliary view, taken along a true-length line in the plane, gives the edge view; a second auxiliary view perpendicular to that edge gives the true shape. None would be enough only if the plane were parallel to a principal plane; one is enough only for an inclined plane, which already appears as an edge in a principal view; three is more than needed.

questions.q: A block has a face that appears as a sloping straight line in the front view and is foreshortened in the plan and end view. Explain how to draw a primary auxiliary view that shows this face at true shape.
markScheme: Recognise the face is inclined and appears as an edge in the front view (1).
Draw a reference line parallel to the edge view of the face (1).
Project from each corner perpendicular to the edge view / reference line (1).
Transfer distances from the reference line in a related view (plan or end view adjacent to the front view) (1).
Join the points; the result is the true shape; optionally draw only the inclined face (partial auxiliary view) (1).
questions.modelAnswer: The face is inclined: it is perpendicular to the frontal plane, so it appears as an edge (a sloping line) in the front view and is foreshortened elsewhere. To see its true shape, view it perpendicular to that edge. Draw a new reference line parallel to the sloping edge, a convenient distance away. From each corner of the face in the front view, project lines perpendicular to the edge, across the new reference line. Each point's distance from the new reference line must equal its depth, that is its distance from the reference line in a related view (the plan, or the end view). Measure those depths and mark them along the projectors. Joining the points gives the face at true shape. It is usual to draw only that face (a partial auxiliary view) to avoid cluttering the view with foreshortened features.

questions.q: In a sectioned assembly, the cutting plane passes along the axis of a shaft and through the housing around it. How is the shaft conventionally shown?
options: Hatched in the opposite direction to the housing
questions.why: Shafts, bolts, pins, keys and similar parts are conventionally not sectioned when cut lengthwise. Hatching in either direction would wrongly treat it as a cut solid region, and solid fill is reserved for material too thin to hatch.

questions.q: Which type of section is drawn in place on a view, rotated through 90°, to show the cross-section of an arm?
questions.why: A revolved section is turned 90° and drawn on the view itself. A removed section shows the same thing but is drawn away from the view; an offset section uses a stepped cutting plane; a half section shows half a symmetrical part in section.

questions.q: State four conventions that apply when presenting a full section view of a single part.
markScheme: Cutting plane shown in an adjacent view with a thin chain line, thick at ends and changes of direction (1).
Arrows give the viewing direction and the section is labelled (e.g. A–A) (1).
Cut material hatched with thin, evenly spaced lines, usually at 45°, the same in every section of that part (1).
Hidden detail behind the plane normally omitted; surfaces seen beyond the plane drawn as visible outlines, not hatched (1).
questions.modelAnswer: First, the cutting plane is shown in an adjacent view by a thin chain line made thick at its ends and wherever it changes direction, with arrows showing which way the section is viewed and letters labelling it, for example A–A; the section view carries the same label. Second, every surface actually cut by the plane is hatched with thin, evenly spaced lines, usually at 45°, and the part keeps that same hatching in every section. Third, edges of surfaces seen beyond the cutting plane are drawn as visible outlines but are not hatched. Fourth, hidden detail behind the plane is normally left out of the section view, since the purpose of sectioning is to make internal features visible.

questions.q: Four features are chain-dimensioned with three dimensions, each toleranced ± 0.05 mm. What is the worst-case variation in the distance between the first and last features?
questions.why: Three chained tolerances add in the worst case: 3 × 0.05 = ± 0.15 mm. ± 0.05 ignores accumulation, ± 0.10 is the datum (parallel) dimensioning result, where the distance between two features picks up only two tolerances, and ± 0.20 counts four links when there are only three dimensions.

questions.q: A stepped bar is dimensioned with each step length and also the overall length, all with tolerances. What is the problem?
questions.why: Giving every step and the overall length closes the chain, so one size is given twice: over-dimensioning, which can make the tolerances contradict each other. Nothing is missing (so not under-dimensioned), and the issue is redundancy, not the use of a datum.

questions.q: A hole is specified as 20.00 to 20.05 mm and the mating shaft as 19.95 to 19.98 mm. Find the maximum and minimum clearance and state the type of fit. Explain briefly why each limit combination gives each result.
markScheme: Minimum clearance = smallest hole − largest shaft (1).
Maximum clearance = largest hole − smallest shaft (1).
Clearance is always positive, so it is a clearance fit (1).
questions.modelAnswer: The tightest assembly occurs with the smallest permitted hole and the largest permitted shaft: 20.00 − 19.98 = 0.02 mm, the minimum clearance. The loosest occurs with the largest hole and the smallest shaft: 20.05 − 19.95 = 0.10 mm, the maximum clearance. Because even the worst case leaves positive clearance (the smallest hole is bigger than the largest shaft), the parts always slide together: it is a clearance fit.

questions.q:
(Practice problem.) Take x to the right, y towards the back and z vertically up. A straight rod runs from A(10, 20, 0) to B(40, 60, 120), all in mm.
(a) Briefly explain where the plan and the view from the left appear relative to the front view in first-angle and in third-angle projection. [4]
(b) Find the apparent length of AB in the front view (x–z plane), the plan (x–y plane) and the end view (y–z plane). [6]
(c) Find the true length of AB and its angles to the horizontal plane and to the frontal (x–z) plane. [5]
(d) Explain how an auxiliary view would show AB at true length, and how you would go on to find the true shape of a triangular plate ABC lying in an oblique plane. [5]
markScheme: (a) First angle: plan below, left view on the right; third angle: plan above, left view on the left (2+2).
(b) Components Δx = 30, Δy = 40, Δz = 120 identified (1).
(c) True length √(30² + 40² + 120²) = 130 mm (2).
(c) Angle to horizontal plane = tan⁻¹(120/50) ≈ 67.4° (equivalently sin⁻¹(120/130)) (2).
(c) Angle to frontal plane = sin⁻¹(40/130) ≈ 17.9° (1).
(d) Reference line parallel to the plan of AB; project perpendicular to it; transfer heights from the front view; AB appears at 130 mm and 67.4° (3).
(d) For ABC: view along a true-length line in the plane to get an edge view, then project perpendicular to the edge view for true shape (2).
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) In first-angle projection each view lies on the side opposite to where it is seen from: the plan is drawn below the front view and the view from the left is drawn to the right of it. In third-angle projection each view lies on the side it is seen from: the plan is above the front view and the view from the left is on the left.

(b) The components of AB are Δx = 40 − 10 = 30 mm, Δy = 60 − 20 = 40 mm and Δz = 120 − 0 = 120 mm. Each view shows the two components parallel to its plane.
Front view (x–z): √(30² + 120²) = √15300 ≈ 123.7 mm.
Plan (x–y): √(30² + 40²) = √2500 = 50 mm.
End view (y–z): √(40² + 120²) = √16000 ≈ 126.5 mm.
All are shorter than the true length, so AB is not parallel to any principal plane.

(c) True length = √(30² + 40² + 120²) = √(900 + 1600 + 14400) = √16900 = 130 mm.
Angle to the horizontal plane: the rise is 120 mm over a plan length of 50 mm, so θ = tan⁻¹(120/50) ≈ 67.4° (check: sin⁻¹(120/130) ≈ 67.4°).
Angle to the frontal (x–z) plane: the component normal to that plane is Δy = 40 mm, so φ = sin⁻¹(40/130) ≈ 17.9°.

(d) Draw a reference line parallel to the plan of AB. Project a and b perpendicular to this line. In the related view (the front view), measure the heights of A and B above the front/plan reference line (0 and 120 mm) and set them off from the new reference line. The auxiliary view is parallel to AB, so a1b1 measures 130 mm and makes 67.4° with the reference line, which is the angle to the horizontal plane.
For a triangular plate ABC in an oblique plane, first find a line in the plate that is true length in an existing view; a horizontal line in the plate is true length in plan. Project an auxiliary view looking along that line, so the line appears as a point and the plate appears as an edge. Then draw a secondary auxiliary view with its reference line parallel to the edge view and project perpendicular to it: the plate appears at true shape.

questions.q:
(Practice problem.) A stepped shaft has three lengths along its axis: A = 40 mm, B = 25 mm and C = 35 mm, giving an overall length of 100 mm. Every length dimension carries a tolerance of ± 0.1 mm.
(a) A draughtsperson dimensions A, B, C and the overall length. What is wrong with this, and how should it be corrected? [4]
(b) If A, B and C are chain-dimensioned and the overall length is not given, find the worst-case limits of the overall length. [4]
(c) The function requires the overall length to be within 100 ± 0.2 mm. Propose a scheme that achieves this using only ± 0.1 mm tolerances, and find the resulting limits of C. [5]
(d) If instead every shoulder is dimensioned from the left-hand end (datum) at 40, 65 and 100 mm, find the worst-case limits of length B. [3]
(e) The shaft's B section, diameter 24.96 to 24.99 mm, runs in a bore of 25.00 to 25.04 mm. Find the minimum and maximum clearance. [4]
markScheme: (a) Over-dimensioned: the closed chain gives a size twice and tolerances can conflict (2); omit one dimension or show it as an untoleranced auxiliary dimension in brackets (2).
(b) Worst case adds tolerances: 100 ± 0.3, i.e. 99.7 to 100.3 mm (4).
(c) Dimension overall length (100 ± 0.1) plus A and B, leaving C undimensioned (2).
(e) Minimum clearance 25.00 − 24.99 = 0.01 mm; maximum 25.04 − 24.96 = 0.08 mm; clearance fit (4).
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Giving A, B, C and the overall length specifies the overall length twice, since it already follows from A + B + C. This is over-dimensioning. Once tolerances are applied the sizes can contradict each other: A, B and C could all be at their upper limits (100.3 mm in total) while the overall dimension allows only up to 100.1 mm. To correct it, leave out the least important dimension in the chain, or show it in brackets as an auxiliary (reference) dimension, which carries no tolerance.

(b) With chain dimensioning the tolerances add in the worst case. Maximum overall = 40.1 + 25.1 + 35.1 = 100.3 mm; minimum = 39.9 + 24.9 + 34.9 = 99.7 mm. So the overall length is 100 ± 0.3 mm.

(c) The overall length is the critical size, so dimension it directly as 100 ± 0.1 mm. That is inside the required ± 0.2. Then dimension A and B (± 0.1 each) and leave C undimensioned, so that C absorbs the accumulated variation. C is largest when the overall length is longest and A and B are shortest: 100.1 − 39.9 − 24.9 = 35.3 mm. C is smallest when the overall length is shortest and A and B are longest: 99.9 − 40.1 − 25.1 = 34.7 mm. So C varies by ± 0.3 mm. That is acceptable only if C is not functionally critical, which is why the least important length should be left out.

(d) With datum dimensioning, B is the difference between two positions measured from the datum: B = (65 ± 0.1) − (40 ± 0.1). Maximum B = 65.1 − 39.9 = 25.2 mm and minimum B = 64.9 − 40.1 = 24.8 mm, so B varies by ± 0.2 mm. Each shoulder's position is held to ± 0.1 mm, but the distance between two shoulders picks up both tolerances.

(e) Minimum clearance = smallest bore − largest shaft = 25.00 − 24.99 = 0.01 mm. Maximum clearance = largest bore − smallest shaft = 25.04 − 24.96 = 0.08 mm. Clearance is positive in every case, so this is a clearance fit.
